prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Individualized Damages Questions Defeat Predominance Under Rule 23(b)(3).**

Rule 23(b)(3) permits certification only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). Predominance is "far more demanding" than commonality. A court must conduct a "rigorous analysis" to decide whether it is met. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 33–34 (2013). Plaintiffs bear the burden of proving each Rule 23 requirement by a preponderance of the evidence. *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811 (7th Cir. 2012). That analysis may require the court to look past the pleadings and into the merits. *Id.* at 811–12.

**A. The Seventh Circuit asks whether individual issues would overwhelm a class trial.**

Defendant acknowledges that "the need for individual damages determinations does not, in and of itself, require denial of a motion to certify a class." *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815. *See also Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013). But that principle has limits, and this case exceeds them. The predominance inquiry asks whether the common questions, once resolved, would leave only a manageable task of individual follow-up. If they would not, the class device offers no efficiency. *See Butler*, 727 F.3d at 801. In *Messner*, the court emphasized that a district court must assess whether the need for individualized proof of injury and damages would swamp any common issues. 669 F.3d at 815–17. Where individual hearings on the amount and fact of loss would dwarf the common questions, certification is improper. *See In re Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc.*, 51 F.3d 1293, 1299–1300 (7th Cir. 1995) (decertifying a class where separate juries would have to resolve individualized issues).

**B. Plaintiffs' damages theory cannot be measured on a classwide basis.**

Plaintiffs must show that damages are "capable of measurement on a classwide basis" and that their model matches their liability theory. *Comcast*, 569 U.S. at 34–35. The Seventh Circuit has applied this requirement and has upheld denial of certification where each class member's loss depends on facts unique to that member. In *Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, 739 F.3d 1083, 1085–86 (7th Cir. 2014), the court recognized that the extent of harm differed from one property to the next. Those differences made a single class proceeding an inefficient way to resolve the claims. *See also Pella Corp. v. Saltzman*, 606 F.3d 391, 394 (7th Cir. 2010) (reversing certification where the products, defects, and resulting harms varied among class members).

Here, each putative class member's recovery would depend on individual circumstances. These include the member's purchasing decisions, the member's use, the member's actual loss, and whether the member suffered any injury. Plaintiffs offer no formula or common method that could resolve these questions without a separate inquiry for each member. The Seventh Circuit has rejected certification in such cases. *See Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 760 (7th Cir. 2014) (explaining that individualized questions of injury and causation can defeat predominance). It has also cautioned that a class definition and damages theory must not rest on assumptions that sweep in uninjured members. *See Kleen Prods. LLC v. Int'l Paper Co.*, 831 F.3d 919, 926–28 (7th Cir. 2016) (stressing the need for rigorous review of whether common evidence can establish classwide impact).

**C. The individual inquiries are intertwined with liability, so they cannot be postponed.**

Plaintiffs may argue that damages can be "bifurcated" and handled after a classwide liability trial. That approach works only when the leftover issues are truly separable and simple. *See Butler*, 727 F.3d at 800–01. It fails when proving that a given member was injured requires the same fact-specific inquiry as quantifying that member's loss. Hundreds or thousands of mini-trials would follow a single common liability ruling. Defendant would also be entitled to contest each member's claim, so the class device would offer neither economy nor fairness. *See Rhone-Poulenc*, 51 F.3d at 1299–1300.

Because individualized damages and injury questions would overwhelm any common questions, Plaintiffs cannot satisfy Rule 23(b)(3). The Court should affirm the denial of class certification.
